title: Shaping How Others Define Success
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article opens with a striking Gallup finding: nearly everyone privately defines success as pursuing one's own talents and interests, yet almost all believe others define success through wealth and fame. The author frames this disconnect as evidence of society's pull toward a homogenized, external definition of success, and argues leaders have a responsibility to counteract it. By repeatedly emphasizing vision, excellence, and personal meaning, and encouraging people to question what popular culture tells them, good leaders can help team members adopt a growth-oriented, more personally grounded definition of achievement, which the piece ties directly to leadership success.
points: A Gallup survey found people privately define success personally, but believe others define it through wealth and fame.
This disconnect reflects society's pull toward external, homogenized measures of success.
Good leaders deliberately talk about vision, excellence, and personal meaning to counter that pull.
Allowing team members to absorb society's definition of success limits their potential.
Shaping a healthier definition of success is framed as core to a leader's own success.
quotes: A recent Gallup survey asked Americans about their view of success.
It is more than curious that people believe others define success very differently than they do.
Fighting the temptation of allowing society to define success is not easy for even the strongest of leaders, but it is essential for your leadership to do so.
Good leaders purposely talk about big-picture abstractions like visions, excellence, and success.
Homogenized thinking is always of a lower quality and is often wrongheaded.
